column4: Autodesk CMO on the three things she looks for when building a team
column10: [Autodesk Chief Marketing Officer Dara Treseder has a big job and needs a strong team around her to do it. In an interview with Yahoo Finance from the 2023 Cannes Lions International Festival, Treseder describes the three things she looks for when she builds her teams.Video TranscriptBRIAN SOZZI: I'm Brian Sozzi, here with Brad Smith, at Cannes Lions. And with a very special guest, Autodesk chief marketing officer, Dara Treseder. Dara, good to meet you in person for a change. I'm a LinkedIn fan.DARA TRESEDER: Oh, thank you. Thank you. It's good to meet you in person as well. I'm a Brian fan.BRIAN SOZZI: Oh. No. It's just-- you know what? I appreciate it. Thank you. So Autodesk, I would argue a lot of people here don't even know what Autodesk does. What is it you have to do, as the CMO, to tell people, this is what we do and here's how we change your life?DARA TRESEDER: It's amazing because Autodesk is how the world gets designed and made. Our software is used to make anything. Whether it is cool cars, amazing movies, games, and even the ads that are winning here at Cannes Lion, many of them were made using Autodesk software. And so it's lovely.I think one of the things that's exciting for me as a chief marketing officer, is start to tell the story of the impact Autodesk is having in the world. How we're helping people make better products, how I'm helping people make more sustainable buildings, how we're really helping to drive more impactful outcomes for businesses, products, and the world.BRIAN SOZZI: I followed your career for a while. And I'm not-- not to be bashful or downplay, but Dara is the one that created these Peloton ads. Crushed it as the chief marketing officer over Peloton. How do you take what you learn there and apply it to a software company like this? Are there similarities, are there differences?DARA TRESEDER: There absolutely are similarities. At the end of the day, when I was going over to Peloton, people were like, you're a BW marketer going over to a B2C company. When I was coming over from Peloton to Autodesk, people were like you're a B2C marketer, what are you doing going to market software?Story continuesThe reality is, until ChatGPT takes over, which hasn't happened yet, we are interacting and talking to humans. And so for me, I think the similarity is, at the end of the day, how are you putting your customer at the center of it all? How are you helping drive your customers' outcomes? It's not about what we want to say or what we want to do, it's about what our customers want to get done. And then how we as marketers enable those delightful experiences to make that happen. So that similarities.Of course, there are nuances. Like when you're in a B2C world, it's all about one to many. That's the game. At Autodesk, it's one-to-one and one to many. We definitely have our e-commerce business, which sits on my team. But we also have the one-to-one relationships, right, the account-based marketing. So it's being able to flex between those two things.BRAD SMITH: We've heard a lot of companies talk about how generative AI is going to boost their bottom line at some point in the future. This is something that's already actively in process at Autodesk.DARA TRESEDER: Yes.BRAD SMITH: How have you been able to flip the switch and make sure that people are able to see the difference right now?DARA TRESEDER: I have to give all the credit to our CEO, Andrew. He's just such a visionary. We have a fusion product, which is used to make anything, right. Tesla cars, for example, are designed and made with our software. It has generative AI built into it, and it always has.And so essentially, if you think about it, it's helping you consider alternative possibilities that you may not have thought about yourself. Kind of the way-- you're kind of seeing it more now with ChatGPT, but that generative AI and generative design has been in Autodesk products, and we're continuing to roll out new products to make that happen.For example, we recently launched Forma, our industry cloud for the architecture industry. And instead of starting from scratch, when you're thinking about concept design, AI can help you get there faster. Connecting workflows and removing those repetitive tasks so you can focus on the creative, exciting aspects of your job.BRIAN SOZZI: Where do these ideas come from? Where do you-- like I said, I've followed your career. How do you come up with creative ideas?DARA TRESEDER: You know, I get inspired by impact. I get inspired by connection. I get inspired by stories that cause people to want to leave things better than they found it. Stories that inspire people to do things differently.And I think at the end of the day, when we think about the power of creativity, to me, it's like pixie dust. It's the thing that makes everything fly. It's the magic. And so inspiration can come from anywhere. But at the heart of it, to me, my inspiration comes from driving impact.BRAD SMITH: At the end of the day too, there's so much creativity out there, talent that's here represented at Cannes Lion events. And as you look across your team that you put around you for a lot of these ambitious ventures, what do you look for?DARA TRESEDER: I look for three things. First is courage. Because, I think, when you do the same things, you get the same results. So when you're trying to drive growth, drive a new wave of growth-- right, we've been through so much uncertainty in the world over the past few years. We're still very much in a period of ambiguity and uncertainty in technology. And so having the courage to be able to take some risks, you have to try things, you have to test, you have to experiment. Intuition will drive testing, but then you need to get that data that will inform your decision-making.Conviction is important. You can have courage, but courage without conviction-- you need to have a point of view. Have a North Star, have a place you want to go, and then have the courage to move there.And, of course, confidence. I think confidence is really important. Because it's easy to start something, it's harder to see it through. And you have to have that confidence because even when things are uncertain, when you've got data, when you are driving impact, you have to have the confidence to be able to see things through.BRIAN SOZZI: In addition to this big title, you're also on the board of Robinhood. These are big, big jobs. You're around a lot of really big leaders. What are some of the challenges companies are up against, looking out over the next 12 months? Is it the economy? Is it a battle versus AI? Is it still finding talent?DARA TRESEDER: I think it's figuring out how to integrate AI to drive better results. It's figuring out how to make sure you've got the best people on your team, and you keep the best people on your team.And it's also figuring out how to navigate uncertainty. It's so difficult when we're kind of in an uncertain environment, to kind of know what to do. And you have to be able to navigate that. And so it's being able to bring those three things together to be able to thrive.BRIAN SOZZI: I will just say, before we let you go, I will say, one, I was late to this interview. It's very busy here. So Dara waited around for a while. I'm never late to anything.DARA TRESEDER: It's OK. I'm not Will.I.Am so--BRIAN SOZZI: Some people will actually say, I will be early to my own funeral. So thank you for waiting, one. And it is raining. We're out here in a live environment in the French Riviera, and it's raining. And you know, I know it looks all beautiful. But thank you for rolling with the punches. We appreciate it.DARA TRESEDER: Thank you so much.BRIAN SOZZI: And congratulations on all your success.DARA TRESEDER: Thank you so much. Really glad to be here.]

column4: Salesforce.com (CRM) Down 1.2% Since Last Earnings Report: Can It Rebound?
column10: [A month has gone by since the last earnings report for Salesforce.com (CRM). Shares have lost about 1.2% in that time frame, underperforming the S&P 500.Will the recent negative trend continue leading up to its next earnings release, or is Salesforce.com due for a breakout? Before we dive into how investors and analysts have reacted as of late, let's take a quick look at its most recent earnings report in order to get a better handle on the important catalysts.Salesforce Q1 Earnings & Sales Beat Estimates, Up Y/YSalesforce reported better-than-expected financial results for the first quarter of fiscal 2024. The enterprise cloud computing solution provider’s first-quarter fiscal 2024 non-GAAP earnings increased 71.4% to $1.69 per share from 98 cents reported in the year-ago quarter. The figure surpassed the Zacks Consensus Estimate of $1.61.The quarterly non-GAAP earnings were adversely impacted by a loss of 11 cents per share from mark-to-mark accounting of CRM’s strategic investments at a non-GAAP tax rate of 23.5%. However, the company’s ongoing restructuring initiative, which includes trimming the workforce, benefited first-quarter non-GAAP earnings by 72 cents per share.Salesforce’s quarterly revenues of $8.25 billion climbed 11% year over year, surpassing the Zacks Consensus Estimate of $8.17 billion. The top line also improved 13% in constant currency.The company has been benefiting from the robust demand environment as customers are undergoing a major digital transformation. Thus, the rapid adoption of its cloud-based solutions resulted in the better-than-anticipated performance in the fiscal first quarter.Quarterly DetailsComing to CRM’s business segments, revenues from Subscription and Support (93% of the total revenues) increased 11.5% from the year-earlier period to $7.64 billion. Professional Services and Other (7% of total sales) revenues climbed 9% to $605 million.Under the Subscription and Support segment, Sales Cloud revenues grew 10.9% year over year to $1.81 billion. Revenues from Service Cloud, one of the company’s largest and fastest-growing businesses, also improved 11.5% to $1.96 billion.Story continuesMarketing & Commerce Cloud revenues jumped 7.4% to $1.17 billion. Salesforce Platform and Other revenues were up 10.4% to $1.57 billion. Also, revenues from Data increased 18.4% year over year to $1.13 billion.Geographically, Salesforce registered revenue growth of 10.3% in America (66.5% of the total revenues), 16% in the Asia Pacific (9.9%) and 12.3% in the EMEA (23.7%) on a year-over-year basis.Salesforce’s gross profit came in at $6.12 billion, up 14.1% from the prior-year period. Moreover, the gross margin improved 200 basis points (bps) to 74%.Salesforce recorded a non-GAAP operating income of $2.27 billion, indicating an increase of 73.9% from the year-ago quarter’s level of $1.31 billion. Moreover, the non-GAAP operating margin expanded 1,000 bps to 27.6% from 17.6% in the year-ago quarter due to lower operating expenses as a percentage of total sales. Operating expenses as a percentage of revenues declined to 69% from 72% in the year-ago quarter.Balance Sheet & Other DetailsSalesforce exited the fiscal first quarter with cash, cash equivalents and marketable securities of $14 billion, up from the $12.5 billion recorded at the end of the previous quarter.CRM generated operating cash flow of $4.49 billion and free cash flow of $4.25 billion in the first quarter.As of Apr 30, 2023, the current remaining performance obligation reflecting revenues under contract for the next 12 months was $24.1 billion, up 12% on a year-over-year basis. In the fiscal first quarter, the company bought back shares worth $2.1 billion. With this buyback of shares, the company has now $9.9 billion remaining under its current authorization limit of $20 billion.Strong Guidance for Q2 and FY24Salesforce provided strong guidance for the second quarter and fiscal 2024. For the fiscal second quarter, Salesforce projects total sales between $8.51 billion and $8.53 billion (midpoint $8.52 billion), indicating 10% year-over-year growth.The company expects no impact on second-quarter revenues from foreign currency exchange rates. Furthermore, CRM anticipates non-GAAP earnings per share in the band of $1.89-$1.90 for the current quarter.For fiscal 2024, Salesforce forecasts revenues in the range of $34.5-$34.7 billion. The company expects no impact from foreign currency exchange rates.The company projects fiscal 2024 non-GAAP earnings between $7.41 and $7.43 per share. Salesforce estimates a non-GAAP operating margin of approximately 28% for fiscal 2024 and expects a year-over-year increase in operating cash flow in the 16-17% range.How Have Estimates Been Moving Since Then?In the past month, investors have witnessed an upward trend in fresh estimates.The consensus estimate has shifted 17.6% due to these changes.VGM ScoresCurrently, Salesforce.com has a strong Growth Score of A, though it is lagging a lot on the Momentum Score front with a D. Charting a somewhat similar path, the stock was allocated a grade of F on the value side, putting it in the lowest quintile for this investment strategy.Overall, the stock has an aggregate VGM Score of C. If you aren't focused on one strategy, this score is the one you should be interested in.OutlookEstimates have been trending upward for the stock, and the magnitude of these revisions looks promising. It comes with little surprise Salesforce.com has a Zacks Rank #1 (Strong Buy). We expect an above average return from the stock in the next few months.Performance of an Industry PlayerSalesforce.com belongs to the Zacks Computer - Software industry. More than a month has passed since the company reported results for the quarter ended April 2023.Autodesk reported revenues of $1.27 billion in the last reported quarter, representing a year-over-year change of +8.5%. EPS of $1.55 for the same period compares with $1.43 a year ago.For the current quarter, Autodesk is expected to post earnings of $1.72 per share, indicating a change of +4.2% from the year-ago quarter. column4: Autodesk CMO on the three things she looks for when building a team
column10: [Autodesk Chief Marketing Officer Dara Treseder has a big job and needs a strong team around her to do it. In an interview with Yahoo Finance from the 2023 Cannes Lions International Festival, Treseder describes the three things she looks for when she builds her teams.Video TranscriptBRIAN SOZZI: I'm Brian Sozzi, here with Brad Smith, at Cannes Lions. And with a very special guest, Autodesk chief marketing officer, Dara Treseder. Dara, good to meet you in person for a change. I'm a LinkedIn fan.DARA TRESEDER: Oh, thank you. Thank you. It's good to meet you in person as well. I'm a Brian fan.BRIAN SOZZI: Oh. No. It's just-- you know what? I appreciate it. Thank you. So Autodesk, I would argue a lot of people here don't even know what Autodesk does. What is it you have to do, as the CMO, to tell people, this is what we do and here's how we change your life?DARA TRESEDER: It's amazing because Autodesk is how the world gets designed and made. Our software is used to make anything. Whether it is cool cars, amazing movies, games, and even the ads that are winning here at Cannes Lion, many of them were made using Autodesk software. And so it's lovely.I think one of the things that's exciting for me as a chief marketing officer, is start to tell the story of the impact Autodesk is having in the world. How we're helping people make better products, how I'm helping people make more sustainable buildings, how we're really helping to drive more impactful outcomes for businesses, products, and the world.BRIAN SOZZI: I followed your career for a while. And I'm not-- not to be bashful or downplay, but Dara is the one that created these Peloton ads. Crushed it as the chief marketing officer over Peloton. How do you take what you learn there and apply it to a software company like this? Are there similarities, are there differences?DARA TRESEDER: There absolutely are similarities. At the end of the day, when I was going over to Peloton, people were like, you're a BW marketer going over to a B2C company. When I was coming over from Peloton to Autodesk, people were like you're a B2C marketer, what are you doing going to market software?Story continuesThe reality is, until ChatGPT takes over, which hasn't happened yet, we are interacting and talking to humans. And so for me, I think the similarity is, at the end of the day, how are you putting your customer at the center of it all? How are you helping drive your customers' outcomes? It's not about what we want to say or what we want to do, it's about what our customers want to get done. And then how we as marketers enable those delightful experiences to make that happen. So that similarities.Of course, there are nuances. Like when you're in a B2C world, it's all about one to many. That's the game. At Autodesk, it's one-to-one and one to many. We definitely have our e-commerce business, which sits on my team. But we also have the one-to-one relationships, right, the account-based marketing. So it's being able to flex between those two things.BRAD SMITH: We've heard a lot of companies talk about how generative AI is going to boost their bottom line at some point in the future. This is something that's already actively in process at Autodesk.DARA TRESEDER: Yes.BRAD SMITH: How have you been able to flip the switch and make sure that people are able to see the difference right now?DARA TRESEDER: I have to give all the credit to our CEO, Andrew. He's just such a visionary. We have a fusion product, which is used to make anything, right. Tesla cars, for example, are designed and made with our software. It has generative AI built into it, and it always has.And so essentially, if you think about it, it's helping you consider alternative possibilities that you may not have thought about yourself. Kind of the way-- you're kind of seeing it more now with ChatGPT, but that generative AI and generative design has been in Autodesk products, and we're continuing to roll out new products to make that happen.For example, we recently launched Forma, our industry cloud for the architecture industry. And instead of starting from scratch, when you're thinking about concept design, AI can help you get there faster. Connecting workflows and removing those repetitive tasks so you can focus on the creative, exciting aspects of your job.BRIAN SOZZI: Where do these ideas come from? Where do you-- like I said, I've followed your career. How do you come up with creative ideas?DARA TRESEDER: You know, I get inspired by impact. I get inspired by connection. I get inspired by stories that cause people to want to leave things better than they found it. Stories that inspire people to do things differently.And I think at the end of the day, when we think about the power of creativity, to me, it's like pixie dust. It's the thing that makes everything fly. It's the magic. And so inspiration can come from anywhere. But at the heart of it, to me, my inspiration comes from driving impact.BRAD SMITH: At the end of the day too, there's so much creativity out there, talent that's here represented at Cannes Lion events. And as you look across your team that you put around you for a lot of these ambitious ventures, what do you look for?DARA TRESEDER: I look for three things. First is courage. Because, I think, when you do the same things, you get the same results. So when you're trying to drive growth, drive a new wave of growth-- right, we've been through so much uncertainty in the world over the past few years. We're still very much in a period of ambiguity and uncertainty in technology. And so having the courage to be able to take some risks, you have to try things, you have to test, you have to experiment. Intuition will drive testing, but then you need to get that data that will inform your decision-making.Conviction is important. You can have courage, but courage without conviction-- you need to have a point of view. Have a North Star, have a place you want to go, and then have the courage to move there.And, of course, confidence. I think confidence is really important. Because it's easy to start something, it's harder to see it through. And you have to have that confidence because even when things are uncertain, when you've got data, when you are driving impact, you have to have the confidence to be able to see things through.BRIAN SOZZI: In addition to this big title, you're also on the board of Robinhood. These are big, big jobs. You're around a lot of really big leaders. What are some of the challenges companies are up against, looking out over the next 12 months? Is it the economy? Is it a battle versus AI? Is it still finding talent?DARA TRESEDER: I think it's figuring out how to integrate AI to drive better results. It's figuring out how to make sure you've got the best people on your team, and you keep the best people on your team.And it's also figuring out how to navigate uncertainty. It's so difficult when we're kind of in an uncertain environment, to kind of know what to do. And you have to be able to navigate that. And so it's being able to bring those three things together to be able to thrive.BRIAN SOZZI: I will just say, before we let you go, I will say, one, I was late to this interview. It's very busy here. So Dara waited around for a while. I'm never late to anything.DARA TRESEDER: It's OK. I'm not Will.I.Am so--BRIAN SOZZI: Some people will actually say, I will be early to my own funeral. So thank you for waiting, one. And it is raining. We're out here in a live environment in the French Riviera, and it's raining. And you know, I know it looks all beautiful. But thank you for rolling with the punches. We appreciate it.DARA TRESEDER: Thank you so much.BRIAN SOZZI: And congratulations on all your success.DARA TRESEDER: Thank you so much. Really glad to be here.]

column10: [A month has gone by since the last earnings report for Salesforce.com (CRM). Before we dive into how investors and analysts have reacted as of late, let's take a quick look at its most recent earnings report in order to get a better handle on the important catalysts.Salesforce Q1 Earnings & Sales Beat Estimates, Up Y/YSalesforce reported better-than-expected financial results for the first quarter of fiscal 2024. The enterprise cloud computing solution provider’s first-quarter fiscal 2024 non-GAAP earnings increased 71.4% to $1.69 per share from 98 cents reported in the year-ago quarter. The figure surpassed the Zacks Consensus Estimate of $1.61.The quarterly non-GAAP earnings were adversely impacted by a loss of 11 cents per share from mark-to-mark accounting of CRM’s strategic investments at a non-GAAP tax rate of 23.5%. However, the company’s ongoing restructuring initiative, which includes trimming the workforce, benefited first-quarter non-GAAP earnings by 72 cents per share.Salesforce’s quarterly revenues of $8.25 billion climbed 11% year over year, surpassing the Zacks Consensus Estimate of $8.17 billion. The top line also improved 13% in constant currency.The company has been benefiting from the robust demand environment as customers are undergoing a major digital transformation. Thus, the rapid adoption of its cloud-based solutions resulted in the better-than-anticipated performance in the fiscal first quarter.Quarterly DetailsComing to CRM’s business segments, revenues from Subscription and Support (93% of the total revenues) increased 11.5% from the year-earlier period to $7.64 billion. Professional Services and Other (7% of total sales) revenues climbed 9% to $605 million.Under the Subscription and Support segment, Sales Cloud revenues grew 10.9% year over year to $1.81 billion. Revenues from Service Cloud, one of the company’s largest and fastest-growing businesses, also improved 11.5% to $1.96 billion.Story continuesMarketing & Commerce Cloud revenues jumped 7.4% to $1.17 billion. Salesforce Platform and Other revenues were up 10.4% to $1.57 billion. Also, revenues from Data increased 18.4% year over year to $1.13 billion.Geographically, Salesforce registered revenue growth of 10.3% in America (66.5% of the total revenues), 16% in the Asia Pacific (9.9%) and 12.3% in the EMEA (23.7%) on a year-over-year basis.Salesforce’s gross profit came in at $6.12 billion, up 14.1% from the prior-year period. Moreover, the gross margin improved 200 basis points (bps) to 74%.Salesforce recorded a non-GAAP operating income of $2.27 billion, indicating an increase of 73.9% from the year-ago quarter’s level of $1.31 billion. Moreover, the non-GAAP operating margin expanded 1,000 bps to 27.6% from 17.6% in the year-ago quarter due to lower operating expenses as a percentage of total sales. Operating expenses as a percentage of revenues declined to 69% from 72% in the year-ago quarter.Balance Sheet & Other DetailsSalesforce exited the fiscal first quarter with cash, cash equivalents and marketable securities of $14 billion, up from the $12.5 billion recorded at the end of the previous quarter.CRM generated operating cash flow of $4.49 billion and free cash flow of $4.25 billion in the first quarter.As of Apr 30, 2023, the current remaining performance obligation reflecting revenues under contract for the next 12 months was $24.1 billion, up 12% on a year-over-year basis. In the fiscal first quarter, the company bought back shares worth $2.1 billion. With this buyback of shares, the company has now $9.9 billion remaining under its current authorization limit of $20 billion.Strong Guidance for Q2 and FY24Salesforce provided strong guidance for the second quarter and fiscal 2024. For the fiscal second quarter, Salesforce projects total sales between $8.51 billion and $8.53 billion (midpoint $8.52 billion), indicating 10% year-over-year growth.The company expects no impact on second-quarter revenues from foreign currency exchange rates. Furthermore, CRM anticipates non-GAAP earnings per share in the band of $1.89-$1.90 for the current quarter.For fiscal 2024, Salesforce forecasts revenues in the range of $34.5-$34.7 billion. The company expects no impact from foreign currency exchange rates.The company projects fiscal 2024 non-GAAP earnings between $7.41 and $7.43 per share. Salesforce estimates a non-GAAP operating margin of approximately 28% for fiscal 2024 and expects a year-over-year increase in operating cash flow in the 16-17% range.How Have Estimates Been Moving Since Then?In the past month, investors have witnessed an upward trend in fresh estimates.The consensus estimate has shifted 17.6% due to these changes.VGM ScoresCurrently, Salesforce.com has a strong Growth Score of A, though it is lagging a lot on the Momentum Score front with a D. column10: [In this article, we will take a look at the 12 best metaverse stocks to invest in. Individuals within the metaverse engage in virtual environments and forge connections with others in the digital realm. Following Facebook's name change to Meta Platforms, Inc. (NASDAQ:META), there was a staggering surge of 7,200% in internet searches for the term 'metaverse'. Once individuals grasp the concept, a significant majority wholeheartedly embrace it: according to recent research conducted by McKinsey, around 60% of consumers express excitement about the metaverse's potential to transform everyday activities such as shopping, dating, and exercising.According to a report by Precedence Research, the global metaverse market accounted for $68.49 billion in 2022 and it is estimated to surpass around $1.3 trillion by 2030 with a registered CAGR of 44.5% during the forecast period 2022 to 2030. While the potential impact of the metaverse varies across industries, it holds implications for all of them. McKinsey, for example, estimates that it may have a market impact of between $2 trillion and $2.6 trillion on e-commerce by 2030. Similarly, an impact of $180 billion to $270 billion on the academic virtual learning market is expected, while a $108 billion to $125 billion impact is anticipated on the gaming market.Overall, this industry is poised to grow with more companies planning to get involved. column4: Autodesk CMO on the three things she looks for when building a team
column10: [Autodesk Chief Marketing Officer Dara Treseder has a big job and needs a strong team around her to do it. In an interview with Yahoo Finance from the 2023 Cannes Lions International Festival, Treseder describes the three things she looks for when she builds her teams.Video TranscriptBRIAN SOZZI: I'm Brian Sozzi, here with Brad Smith, at Cannes Lions. And with a very special guest, Autodesk chief marketing officer, Dara Treseder. Dara, good to meet you in person for a change. I'm a LinkedIn fan.DARA TRESEDER: Oh, thank you. Thank you. It's good to meet you in person as well. I'm a Brian fan.BRIAN SOZZI: Oh. No. It's just-- you know what? I appreciate it. Thank you. So Autodesk, I would argue a lot of people here don't even know what Autodesk does. What is it you have to do, as the CMO, to tell people, this is what we do and here's how we change your life?DARA TRESEDER: It's amazing because Autodesk is how the world gets designed and made. Our software is used to make anything. Whether it is cool cars, amazing movies, games, and even the ads that are winning here at Cannes Lion, many of them were made using Autodesk software. And so it's lovely.I think one of the things that's exciting for me as a chief marketing officer, is start to tell the story of the impact Autodesk is having in the world. How we're helping people make better products, how I'm helping people make more sustainable buildings, how we're really helping to drive more impactful outcomes for businesses, products, and the world.BRIAN SOZZI: I followed your career for a while. And I'm not-- not to be bashful or downplay, but Dara is the one that created these Peloton ads. Crushed it as the chief marketing officer over Peloton. How do you take what you learn there and apply it to a software company like this? Are there similarities, are there differences?DARA TRESEDER: There absolutely are similarities. At the end of the day, when I was going over to Peloton, people were like, you're a BW marketer going over to a B2C company. When I was coming over from Peloton to Autodesk, people were like you're a B2C marketer, what are you doing going to market software?Story continuesThe reality is, until ChatGPT takes over, which hasn't happened yet, we are interacting and talking to humans. And so for me, I think the similarity is, at the end of the day, how are you putting your customer at the center of it all? How are you helping drive your customers' outcomes? It's not about what we want to say or what we want to do, it's about what our customers want to get done. And then how we as marketers enable those delightful experiences to make that happen. So that similarities.Of course, there are nuances. Like when you're in a B2C world, it's all about one to many. That's the game. At Autodesk, it's one-to-one and one to many. We definitely have our e-commerce business, which sits on my team. But we also have the one-to-one relationships, right, the account-based marketing. So it's being able to flex between those two things.BRAD SMITH: We've heard a lot of companies talk about how generative AI is going to boost their bottom line at some point in the future. This is something that's already actively in process at Autodesk.DARA TRESEDER: Yes.BRAD SMITH: How have you been able to flip the switch and make sure that people are able to see the difference right now?DARA TRESEDER: I have to give all the credit to our CEO, Andrew. He's just such a visionary. We have a fusion product, which is used to make anything, right. Tesla cars, for example, are designed and made with our software. It has generative AI built into it, and it always has.And so essentially, if you think about it, it's helping you consider alternative possibilities that you may not have thought about yourself. Kind of the way-- you're kind of seeing it more now with ChatGPT, but that generative AI and generative design has been in Autodesk products, and we're continuing to roll out new products to make that happen.For example, we recently launched Forma, our industry cloud for the architecture industry. And instead of starting from scratch, when you're thinking about concept design, AI can help you get there faster. Connecting workflows and removing those repetitive tasks so you can focus on the creative, exciting aspects of your job.BRIAN SOZZI: Where do these ideas come from? Where do you-- like I said, I've followed your career. How do you come up with creative ideas?DARA TRESEDER: You know, I get inspired by impact. I get inspired by connection. I get inspired by stories that cause people to want to leave things better than they found it. Stories that inspire people to do things differently.And I think at the end of the day, when we think about the power of creativity, to me, it's like pixie dust. It's the thing that makes everything fly. It's the magic. And so inspiration can come from anywhere. But at the heart of it, to me, my inspiration comes from driving impact.BRAD SMITH: At the end of the day too, there's so much creativity out there, talent that's here represented at Cannes Lion events. And as you look across your team that you put around you for a lot of these ambitious ventures, what do you look for?DARA TRESEDER: I look for three things. First is courage. Because, I think, when you do the same things, you get the same results. So when you're trying to drive growth, drive a new wave of growth-- right, we've been through so much uncertainty in the world over the past few years. We're still very much in a period of ambiguity and uncertainty in technology. And so having the courage to be able to take some risks, you have to try things, you have to test, you have to experiment. Intuition will drive testing, but then you need to get that data that will inform your decision-making.Conviction is important. You can have courage, but courage without conviction-- you need to have a point of view. Have a North Star, have a place you want to go, and then have the courage to move there.And, of course, confidence. I think confidence is really important. Because it's easy to start something, it's harder to see it through. And you have to have that confidence because even when things are uncertain, when you've got data, when you are driving impact, you have to have the confidence to be able to see things through.BRIAN SOZZI: In addition to this big title, you're also on the board of Robinhood. These are big, big jobs. You're around a lot of really big leaders. What are some of the challenges companies are up against, looking out over the next 12 months? Is it the economy? Is it a battle versus AI? Is it still finding talent?DARA TRESEDER: I think it's figuring out how to integrate AI to drive better results. It's figuring out how to make sure you've got the best people on your team, and you keep the best people on your team.And it's also figuring out how to navigate uncertainty. It's so difficult when we're kind of in an uncertain environment, to kind of know what to do. And you have to be able to navigate that. And so it's being able to bring those three things together to be able to thrive.BRIAN SOZZI: I will just say, before we let you go, I will say, one, I was late to this interview. It's very busy here. So Dara waited around for a while. I'm never late to anything.DARA TRESEDER: It's OK. I'm not Will.I.Am so--BRIAN SOZZI: Some people will actually say, I will be early to my own funeral. So thank you for waiting, one. And it is raining. We're out here in a live environment in the French Riviera, and it's raining. And you know, I know it looks all beautiful. But thank you for rolling with the punches. We appreciate it.DARA TRESEDER: Thank you so much.BRIAN SOZZI: And congratulations on all your success.DARA TRESEDER: Thank you so much. Really glad to be here.]

column4: Salesforce.com (CRM) Down 1.2% Since Last Earnings Report: Can It Rebound?
column10: [A month has gone by since the last earnings report for Salesforce.com (CRM). Shares have lost about 1.2% in that time frame, underperforming the S&P 500.Will the recent negative trend continue leading up to its next earnings release, or is Salesforce.com due for a breakout? Before we dive into how investors and analysts have reacted as of late, let's take a quick look at its most recent earnings report in order to get a better handle on the important catalysts.Salesforce Q1 Earnings & Sales Beat Estimates, Up Y/YSalesforce reported better-than-expected financial results for the first quarter of fiscal 2024. The enterprise cloud computing solution provider’s first-quarter fiscal 2024 non-GAAP earnings increased 71.4% to $1.69 per share from 98 cents reported in the year-ago quarter. The figure surpassed the Zacks Consensus Estimate of $1.61.The quarterly non-GAAP earnings were adversely impacted by a loss of 11 cents per share from mark-to-mark accounting of CRM’s strategic investments at a non-GAAP tax rate of 23.5%. However, the company’s ongoing restructuring initiative, which includes trimming the workforce, benefited first-quarter non-GAAP earnings by 72 cents per share.Salesforce’s quarterly revenues of $8.25 billion climbed 11% year over year, surpassing the Zacks Consensus Estimate of $8.17 billion. The top line also improved 13% in constant currency.The company has been benefiting from the robust demand environment as customers are undergoing a major digital transformation. Thus, the rapid adoption of its cloud-based solutions resulted in the better-than-anticipated performance in the fiscal first quarter.Quarterly DetailsComing to CRM’s business segments, revenues from Subscription and Support (93% of the total revenues) increased 11.5% from the year-earlier period to $7.64 billion. Professional Services and Other (7% of total sales) revenues climbed 9% to $605 million.Under the Subscription and Support segment, Sales Cloud revenues grew 10.9% year over year to $1.81 billion. Revenues from Service Cloud, one of the company’s largest and fastest-growing businesses, also improved 11.5% to $1.96 billion.Story continuesMarketing & Commerce Cloud revenues jumped 7.4% to $1.17 billion. Salesforce Platform and Other revenues were up 10.4% to $1.57 billion. Also, revenues from Data increased 18.4% year over year to $1.13 billion.Geographically, Salesforce registered revenue growth of 10.3% in America (66.5% of the total revenues), 16% in the Asia Pacific (9.9%) and 12.3% in the EMEA (23.7%) on a year-over-year basis.Salesforce’s gross profit came in at $6.12 billion, up 14.1% from the prior-year period. Moreover, the gross margin improved 200 basis points (bps) to 74%.Salesforce recorded a non-GAAP operating income of $2.27 billion, indicating an increase of 73.9% from the year-ago quarter’s level of $1.31 billion. Moreover, the non-GAAP operating margin expanded 1,000 bps to 27.6% from 17.6% in the year-ago quarter due to lower operating expenses as a percentage of total sales. Operating expenses as a percentage of revenues declined to 69% from 72% in the year-ago quarter.Balance Sheet & Other DetailsSalesforce exited the fiscal first quarter with cash, cash equivalents and marketable securities of $14 billion, up from the $12.5 billion recorded at the end of the previous quarter.CRM generated operating cash flow of $4.49 billion and free cash flow of $4.25 billion in the first quarter.As of Apr 30, 2023, the current remaining performance obligation reflecting revenues under contract for the next 12 months was $24.1 billion, up 12% on a year-over-year basis. In the fiscal first quarter, the company bought back shares worth $2.1 billion. With this buyback of shares, the company has now $9.9 billion remaining under its current authorization limit of $20 billion.Strong Guidance for Q2 and FY24Salesforce provided strong guidance for the second quarter and fiscal 2024. For the fiscal second quarter, Salesforce projects total sales between $8.51 billion and $8.53 billion (midpoint $8.52 billion), indicating 10% year-over-year growth.The company expects no impact on second-quarter revenues from foreign currency exchange rates. Furthermore, CRM anticipates non-GAAP earnings per share in the band of $1.89-$1.90 for the current quarter.For fiscal 2024, Salesforce forecasts revenues in the range of $34.5-$34.7 billion. The company expects no impact from foreign currency exchange rates.The company projects fiscal 2024 non-GAAP earnings between $7.41 and $7.43 per share. Salesforce estimates a non-GAAP operating margin of approximately 28% for fiscal 2024 and expects a year-over-year increase in operating cash flow in the 16-17% range.How Have Estimates Been Moving Since Then?In the past month, investors have witnessed an upward trend in fresh estimates.The consensus estimate has shifted 17.6% due to these changes.VGM ScoresCurrently, Salesforce.com has a strong Growth Score of A, though it is lagging a lot on the Momentum Score front with a D. column4: Autodesk CMO on the three things she looks for when building a team
column10: [Autodesk Chief Marketing Officer Dara Treseder has a big job and needs a strong team around her to do it. In an interview with Yahoo Finance from the 2023 Cannes Lions International Festival, Treseder describes the three things she looks for when she builds her teams.Video TranscriptBRIAN SOZZI: I'm Brian Sozzi, here with Brad Smith, at Cannes Lions. And with a very special guest, Autodesk chief marketing officer, Dara Treseder. Dara, good to meet you in person for a change. I'm a LinkedIn fan.DARA TRESEDER: Oh, thank you. Thank you. It's good to meet you in person as well. I'm a Brian fan.BRIAN SOZZI: Oh. No. It's just-- you know what? I appreciate it. Thank you. So Autodesk, I would argue a lot of people here don't even know what Autodesk does. What is it you have to do, as the CMO, to tell people, this is what we do and here's how we change your life?DARA TRESEDER: It's amazing because Autodesk is how the world gets designed and made. Our software is used to make anything. Whether it is cool cars, amazing movies, games, and even the ads that are winning here at Cannes Lion, many of them were made using Autodesk software. And so it's lovely.I think one of the things that's exciting for me as a chief marketing officer, is start to tell the story of the impact Autodesk is having in the world. How we're helping people make better products, how I'm helping people make more sustainable buildings, how we're really helping to drive more impactful outcomes for businesses, products, and the world.BRIAN SOZZI: I followed your career for a while. And I'm not-- not to be bashful or downplay, but Dara is the one that created these Peloton ads. Crushed it as the chief marketing officer over Peloton. How do you take what you learn there and apply it to a software company like this? Are there similarities, are there differences?DARA TRESEDER: There absolutely are similarities. At the end of the day, when I was going over to Peloton, people were like, you're a BW marketer going over to a B2C company. When I was coming over from Peloton to Autodesk, people were like you're a B2C marketer, what are you doing going to market software?Story continuesThe reality is, until ChatGPT takes over, which hasn't happened yet, we are interacting and talking to humans. And so for me, I think the similarity is, at the end of the day, how are you putting your customer at the center of it all? How are you helping drive your customers' outcomes? It's not about what we want to say or what we want to do, it's about what our customers want to get done. And then how we as marketers enable those delightful experiences to make that happen. So that similarities.Of course, there are nuances. Like when you're in a B2C world, it's all about one to many. That's the game. At Autodesk, it's one-to-one and one to many. We definitely have our e-commerce business, which sits on my team. But we also have the one-to-one relationships, right, the account-based marketing. So it's being able to flex between those two things.BRAD SMITH: We've heard a lot of companies talk about how generative AI is going to boost their bottom line at some point in the future. This is something that's already actively in process at Autodesk.DARA TRESEDER: Yes.BRAD SMITH: How have you been able to flip the switch and make sure that people are able to see the difference right now?DARA TRESEDER: I have to give all the credit to our CEO, Andrew. He's just such a visionary. We have a fusion product, which is used to make anything, right. Tesla cars, for example, are designed and made with our software. It has generative AI built into it, and it always has.And so essentially, if you think about it, it's helping you consider alternative possibilities that you may not have thought about yourself. Kind of the way-- you're kind of seeing it more now with ChatGPT, but that generative AI and generative design has been in Autodesk products, and we're continuing to roll out new products to make that happen.For example, we recently launched Forma, our industry cloud for the architecture industry. And instead of starting from scratch, when you're thinking about concept design, AI can help you get there faster. Connecting workflows and removing those repetitive tasks so you can focus on the creative, exciting aspects of your job.BRIAN SOZZI: Where do these ideas come from? Where do you-- like I said, I've followed your career. How do you come up with creative ideas?DARA TRESEDER: You know, I get inspired by impact. I get inspired by connection. I get inspired by stories that cause people to want to leave things better than they found it. Stories that inspire people to do things differently.And I think at the end of the day, when we think about the power of creativity, to me, it's like pixie dust. It's the thing that makes everything fly. It's the magic. And so inspiration can come from anywhere. But at the heart of it, to me, my inspiration comes from driving impact.BRAD SMITH: At the end of the day too, there's so much creativity out there, talent that's here represented at Cannes Lion events. And as you look across your team that you put around you for a lot of these ambitious ventures, what do you look for?DARA TRESEDER: I look for three things. First is courage. Because, I think, when you do the same things, you get the same results. So when you're trying to drive growth, drive a new wave of growth-- right, we've been through so much uncertainty in the world over the past few years. We're still very much in a period of ambiguity and uncertainty in technology. And so having the courage to be able to take some risks, you have to try things, you have to test, you have to experiment. Intuition will drive testing, but then you need to get that data that will inform your decision-making.Conviction is important. You can have courage, but courage without conviction-- you need to have a point of view. Have a North Star, have a place you want to go, and then have the courage to move there.And, of course, confidence. I think confidence is really important. Because it's easy to start something, it's harder to see it through. And you have to have that confidence because even when things are uncertain, when you've got data, when you are driving impact, you have to have the confidence to be able to see things through.BRIAN SOZZI: In addition to this big title, you're also on the board of Robinhood. These are big, big jobs. You're around a lot of really big leaders. What are some of the challenges companies are up against, looking out over the next 12 months? Is it the economy? Is it a battle versus AI? Is it still finding talent?DARA TRESEDER: I think it's figuring out how to integrate AI to drive better results. It's figuring out how to make sure you've got the best people on your team, and you keep the best people on your team.And it's also figuring out how to navigate uncertainty. It's so difficult when we're kind of in an uncertain environment, to kind of know what to do. And you have to be able to navigate that. And so it's being able to bring those three things together to be able to thrive.BRIAN SOZZI: I will just say, before we let you go, I will say, one, I was late to this interview. It's very busy here. So Dara waited around for a while. I'm never late to anything.DARA TRESEDER: It's OK. I'm not Will.I.Am so--BRIAN SOZZI: Some people will actually say, I will be early to my own funeral. So thank you for waiting, one. And it is raining. We're out here in a live environment in the French Riviera, and it's raining. And you know, I know it looks all beautiful. But thank you for rolling with the punches. We appreciate it.DARA TRESEDER: Thank you so much.BRIAN SOZZI: And congratulations on all your success.DARA TRESEDER: Thank you so much. Really glad to be here.]

column10: [A month has gone by since the last earnings report for Salesforce.com (CRM). The enterprise cloud computing solution provider’s first-quarter fiscal 2024 non-GAAP earnings increased 71.4% to $1.69 per share from 98 cents reported in the year-ago quarter. The figure surpassed the Zacks Consensus Estimate of $1.61.The quarterly non-GAAP earnings were adversely impacted by a loss of 11 cents per share from mark-to-mark accounting of CRM’s strategic investments at a non-GAAP tax rate of 23.5%. However, the company’s ongoing restructuring initiative, which includes trimming the workforce, benefited first-quarter non-GAAP earnings by 72 cents per share.Salesforce’s quarterly revenues of $8.25 billion climbed 11% year over year, surpassing the Zacks Consensus Estimate of $8.17 billion. The top line also improved 13% in constant currency.The company has been benefiting from the robust demand environment as customers are undergoing a major digital transformation. Thus, the rapid adoption of its cloud-based solutions resulted in the better-than-anticipated performance in the fiscal first quarter.Quarterly DetailsComing to CRM’s business segments, revenues from Subscription and Support (93% of the total revenues) increased 11.5% from the year-earlier period to $7.64 billion. Professional Services and Other (7% of total sales) revenues climbed 9% to $605 million.Under the Subscription and Support segment, Sales Cloud revenues grew 10.9% year over year to $1.81 billion. Revenues from Service Cloud, one of the company’s largest and fastest-growing businesses, also improved 11.5% to $1.96 billion.Story continuesMarketing & Commerce Cloud revenues jumped 7.4% to $1.17 billion. Salesforce Platform and Other revenues were up 10.4% to $1.57 billion. Also, revenues from Data increased 18.4% year over year to $1.13 billion.Geographically, Salesforce registered revenue growth of 10.3% in America (66.5% of the total revenues), 16% in the Asia Pacific (9.9%) and 12.3% in the EMEA (23.7%) on a year-over-year basis.Salesforce’s gross profit came in at $6.12 billion, up 14.1% from the prior-year period. Moreover, the gross margin improved 200 basis points (bps) to 74%.Salesforce recorded a non-GAAP operating income of $2.27 billion, indicating an increase of 73.9% from the year-ago quarter’s level of $1.31 billion. Moreover, the non-GAAP operating margin expanded 1,000 bps to 27.6% from 17.6% in the year-ago quarter due to lower operating expenses as a percentage of total sales. Operating expenses as a percentage of revenues declined to 69% from 72% in the year-ago quarter.Balance Sheet & Other DetailsSalesforce exited the fiscal first quarter with cash, cash equivalents and marketable securities of $14 billion, up from the $12.5 billion recorded at the end of the previous quarter.CRM generated operating cash flow of $4.49 billion and free cash flow of $4.25 billion in the first quarter.As of Apr 30, 2023, the current remaining performance obligation reflecting revenues under contract for the next 12 months was $24.1 billion, up 12% on a year-over-year basis. In the fiscal first quarter, the company bought back shares worth $2.1 billion. With this buyback of shares, the company has now $9.9 billion remaining under its current authorization limit of $20 billion.Strong Guidance for Q2 and FY24Salesforce provided strong guidance for the second quarter and fiscal 2024. For the fiscal second quarter, Salesforce projects total sales between $8.51 billion and $8.53 billion (midpoint $8.52 billion), indicating 10% year-over-year growth.The company expects no impact on second-quarter revenues from foreign currency exchange rates. Furthermore, CRM anticipates non-GAAP earnings per share in the band of $1.89-$1.90 for the current quarter.For fiscal 2024, Salesforce forecasts revenues in the range of $34.5-$34.7 billion. The company expects no impact from foreign currency exchange rates.The company projects fiscal 2024 non-GAAP earnings between $7.41 and $7.43 per share. Salesforce estimates a non-GAAP operating margin of approximately 28% for fiscal 2024 and expects a year-over-year increase in operating cash flow in the 16-17% range.How Have Estimates Been Moving Since Then?In the past month, investors have witnessed an upward trend in fresh estimates.The consensus estimate has shifted 17.6% due to these changes.VGM ScoresCurrently, Salesforce.com has a strong Growth Score of A, though it is lagging a lot on the Momentum Score front with a D. If you aren't focused on one strategy, this score is the one you should be interested in.OutlookEstimates have been trending upward for the stock, and the magnitude of these revisions looks promising. It comes with little surprise Salesforce.com has a Zacks Rank #1 (Strong Buy). column4: Autodesk CMO on the three things she looks for when building a team
column10: [Autodesk Chief Marketing Officer Dara Treseder has a big job and needs a strong team around her to do it. In an interview with Yahoo Finance from the 2023 Cannes Lions International Festival, Treseder describes the three things she looks for when she builds her teams.Video TranscriptBRIAN SOZZI: I'm Brian Sozzi, here with Brad Smith, at Cannes Lions. And with a very special guest, Autodesk chief marketing officer, Dara Treseder. Dara, good to meet you in person for a change. I'm a LinkedIn fan.DARA TRESEDER: Oh, thank you. Thank you. It's good to meet you in person as well. I'm a Brian fan.BRIAN SOZZI: Oh. No. It's just-- you know what? I appreciate it. Thank you. So Autodesk, I would argue a lot of people here don't even know what Autodesk does. What is it you have to do, as the CMO, to tell people, this is what we do and here's how we change your life?DARA TRESEDER: It's amazing because Autodesk is how the world gets designed and made. Our software is used to make anything. Whether it is cool cars, amazing movies, games, and even the ads that are winning here at Cannes Lion, many of them were made using Autodesk software. And so it's lovely.I think one of the things that's exciting for me as a chief marketing officer, is start to tell the story of the impact Autodesk is having in the world. How we're helping people make better products, how I'm helping people make more sustainable buildings, how we're really helping to drive more impactful outcomes for businesses, products, and the world.BRIAN SOZZI: I followed your career for a while. And I'm not-- not to be bashful or downplay, but Dara is the one that created these Peloton ads. Crushed it as the chief marketing officer over Peloton. How do you take what you learn there and apply it to a software company like this? Are there similarities, are there differences?DARA TRESEDER: There absolutely are similarities. At the end of the day, when I was going over to Peloton, people were like, you're a BW marketer going over to a B2C company. When I was coming over from Peloton to Autodesk, people were like you're a B2C marketer, what are you doing going to market software?Story continuesThe reality is, until ChatGPT takes over, which hasn't happened yet, we are interacting and talking to humans. And so for me, I think the similarity is, at the end of the day, how are you putting your customer at the center of it all? How are you helping drive your customers' outcomes? It's not about what we want to say or what we want to do, it's about what our customers want to get done. And then how we as marketers enable those delightful experiences to make that happen. So that similarities.Of course, there are nuances. Like when you're in a B2C world, it's all about one to many. That's the game. At Autodesk, it's one-to-one and one to many. We definitely have our e-commerce business, which sits on my team. But we also have the one-to-one relationships, right, the account-based marketing. So it's being able to flex between those two things.BRAD SMITH: We've heard a lot of companies talk about how generative AI is going to boost their bottom line at some point in the future. This is something that's already actively in process at Autodesk.DARA TRESEDER: Yes.BRAD SMITH: How have you been able to flip the switch and make sure that people are able to see the difference right now?DARA TRESEDER: I have to give all the credit to our CEO, Andrew. He's just such a visionary. We have a fusion product, which is used to make anything, right. Tesla cars, for example, are designed and made with our software. It has generative AI built into it, and it always has.And so essentially, if you think about it, it's helping you consider alternative possibilities that you may not have thought about yourself. Kind of the way-- you're kind of seeing it more now with ChatGPT, but that generative AI and generative design has been in Autodesk products, and we're continuing to roll out new products to make that happen.For example, we recently launched Forma, our industry cloud for the architecture industry. And instead of starting from scratch, when you're thinking about concept design, AI can help you get there faster. Connecting workflows and removing those repetitive tasks so you can focus on the creative, exciting aspects of your job.BRIAN SOZZI: Where do these ideas come from? Where do you-- like I said, I've followed your career. How do you come up with creative ideas?DARA TRESEDER: You know, I get inspired by impact. I get inspired by connection. I get inspired by stories that cause people to want to leave things better than they found it. Stories that inspire people to do things differently.And I think at the end of the day, when we think about the power of creativity, to me, it's like pixie dust. It's the thing that makes everything fly. It's the magic. And so inspiration can come from anywhere. But at the heart of it, to me, my inspiration comes from driving impact.BRAD SMITH: At the end of the day too, there's so much creativity out there, talent that's here represented at Cannes Lion events. And as you look across your team that you put around you for a lot of these ambitious ventures, what do you look for?DARA TRESEDER: I look for three things. First is courage. Because, I think, when you do the same things, you get the same results. So when you're trying to drive growth, drive a new wave of growth-- right, we've been through so much uncertainty in the world over the past few years. We're still very much in a period of ambiguity and uncertainty in technology. And so having the courage to be able to take some risks, you have to try things, you have to test, you have to experiment. Intuition will drive testing, but then you need to get that data that will inform your decision-making.Conviction is important. You can have courage, but courage without conviction-- you need to have a point of view. Have a North Star, have a place you want to go, and then have the courage to move there.And, of course, confidence. I think confidence is really important. Because it's easy to start something, it's harder to see it through. And you have to have that confidence because even when things are uncertain, when you've got data, when you are driving impact, you have to have the confidence to be able to see things through.BRIAN SOZZI: In addition to this big title, you're also on the board of Robinhood. These are big, big jobs. You're around a lot of really big leaders. What are some of the challenges companies are up against, looking out over the next 12 months? Is it the economy? Is it a battle versus AI? Is it still finding talent?DARA TRESEDER: I think it's figuring out how to integrate AI to drive better results. It's figuring out how to make sure you've got the best people on your team, and you keep the best people on your team.And it's also figuring out how to navigate uncertainty. It's so difficult when we're kind of in an uncertain environment, to kind of know what to do. And you have to be able to navigate that. And so it's being able to bring those three things together to be able to thrive.BRIAN SOZZI: I will just say, before we let you go, I will say, one, I was late to this interview. It's very busy here. So Dara waited around for a while. I'm never late to anything.DARA TRESEDER: It's OK. I'm not Will.I.Am so--BRIAN SOZZI: Some people will actually say, I will be early to my own funeral. So thank you for waiting, one. And it is raining. We're out here in a live environment in the French Riviera, and it's raining. And you know, I know it looks all beautiful. But thank you for rolling with the punches. We appreciate it.DARA TRESEDER: Thank you so much.BRIAN SOZZI: And congratulations on all your success.DARA TRESEDER: Thank you so much. Really glad to be here.]

The figure surpassed the Zacks Consensus Estimate of $1.61.The quarterly non-GAAP earnings were adversely impacted by a loss of 11 cents per share from mark-to-mark accounting of CRM’s strategic investments at a non-GAAP tax rate of 23.5%. However, the company’s ongoing restructuring initiative, which includes trimming the workforce, benefited first-quarter non-GAAP earnings by 72 cents per share.Salesforce’s quarterly revenues of $8.25 billion climbed 11% year over year, surpassing the Zacks Consensus Estimate of $8.17 billion. The top line also improved 13% in constant currency.The company has been benefiting from the robust demand environment as customers are undergoing a major digital transformation. Thus, the rapid adoption of its cloud-based solutions resulted in the better-than-anticipated performance in the fiscal first quarter.Quarterly DetailsComing to CRM’s business segments, revenues from Subscription and Support (93% of the total revenues) increased 11.5% from the year-earlier period to $7.64 billion. Professional Services and Other (7% of total sales) revenues climbed 9% to $605 million.Under the Subscription and Support segment, Sales Cloud revenues grew 10.9% year over year to $1.81 billion. Revenues from Service Cloud, one of the company’s largest and fastest-growing businesses, also improved 11.5% to $1.96 billion.Story continuesMarketing & Commerce Cloud revenues jumped 7.4% to $1.17 billion. Salesforce Platform and Other revenues were up 10.4% to $1.57 billion. Also, revenues from Data increased 18.4% year over year to $1.13 billion.Geographically, Salesforce registered revenue growth of 10.3% in America (66.5% of the total revenues), 16% in the Asia Pacific (9.9%) and 12.3% in the EMEA (23.7%) on a year-over-year basis.Salesforce’s gross profit came in at $6.12 billion, up 14.1% from the prior-year period. Moreover, the gross margin improved 200 basis points (bps) to 74%.Salesforce recorded a non-GAAP operating income of $2.27 billion, indicating an increase of 73.9% from the year-ago quarter’s level of $1.31 billion. Moreover, the non-GAAP operating margin expanded 1,000 bps to 27.6% from 17.6% in the year-ago quarter due to lower operating expenses as a percentage of total sales. Operating expenses as a percentage of revenues declined to 69% from 72% in the year-ago quarter.Balance Sheet & Other DetailsSalesforce exited the fiscal first quarter with cash, cash equivalents and marketable securities of $14 billion, up from the $12.5 billion recorded at the end of the previous quarter.CRM generated operating cash flow of $4.49 billion and free cash flow of $4.25 billion in the first quarter.As of Apr 30, 2023, the current remaining performance obligation reflecting revenues under contract for the next 12 months was $24.1 billion, up 12% on a year-over-year basis. In the fiscal first quarter, the company bought back shares worth $2.1 billion. With this buyback of shares, the company has now $9.9 billion remaining under its current authorization limit of $20 billion.Strong Guidance for Q2 and FY24Salesforce provided strong guidance for the second quarter and fiscal 2024. For the fiscal second quarter, Salesforce projects total sales between $8.51 billion and $8.53 billion (midpoint $8.52 billion), indicating 10% year-over-year growth.The company expects no impact on second-quarter revenues from foreign currency exchange rates. Furthermore, CRM anticipates non-GAAP earnings per share in the band of $1.89-$1.90 for the current quarter.For fiscal 2024, Salesforce forecasts revenues in the range of $34.5-$34.7 billion. The company expects no impact from foreign currency exchange rates.The company projects fiscal 2024 non-GAAP earnings between $7.41 and $7.43 per share. Salesforce estimates a non-GAAP operating margin of approximately 28% for fiscal 2024 and expects a year-over-year increase in operating cash flow in the 16-17% range.How Have Estimates Been Moving Since Then?In the past month, investors have witnessed an upward trend in fresh estimates.The consensus estimate has shifted 17.6% due to these changes.VGM ScoresCurrently, Salesforce.com has a strong Growth Score of A, though it is lagging a lot on the Momentum Score front with a D. column4: 12 Best Metaverse Stocks To Invest In
column10: [In this article, we will take a look at the 12 best metaverse stocks to invest in. To skip our detailed analysis of the Metaverse and its advancements, go directly to 5 Best Metaverse Stocks To Invest In.While the idea of a real-life "Matrix" may appear to belong solely to the realm of science fiction, it is important to remember that notions such as self-driving cars, smartphones, and even the internet itself were once deemed fantastical concepts too. The metaverse, a digital sphere still in its early evolution, is an immersive three-dimensional universe that has become a hot topic in the world of technology. Individuals within the metaverse engage in virtual environments and forge connections with others in the digital realm. Following Facebook's name change to Meta Platforms, Inc. (NASDAQ:META), there was a staggering surge of 7,200% in internet searches for the term 'metaverse'. Once individuals grasp the concept, a significant majority wholeheartedly embrace it: according to recent research conducted by McKinsey, around 60% of consumers express excitement about the metaverse's potential to transform everyday activities such as shopping, dating, and exercising.According to a report by Precedence Research, the global metaverse market accounted for $68.49 billion in 2022 and it is estimated to surpass around $1.3 trillion by 2030 with a registered CAGR of 44.5% during the forecast period 2022 to 2030. While the potential impact of the metaverse varies across industries, it holds implications for all of them. McKinsey, for example, estimates that it may have a market impact of between $2 trillion and $2.6 trillion on e-commerce by 2030. Similarly, an impact of $180 billion to $270 billion on the academic virtual learning market is expected, while a $108 billion to $125 billion impact is anticipated on the gaming market.Overall, this industry is poised to grow with more companies planning to get involved. The technologies that are involved with the metaverse can include virtual reality (VR), characterized by persistent virtual worlds that continue to exist even when you are not playing, as well as augmented reality (AR) that combines aspects of the digital and physical worlds. Companies like Amazon.com, Inc. (NASDAQ:AMZN), Microsoft Corporation (NASDAQ:MSFT), and NVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ:NVDA) are among the many that are making strides in the space and could be at the forefront of the metaverse's massive opportunity. (NYSE:U) has revised its fiscal 2023 outlook, anticipating even stronger results that are poised to surpass estimates. (NYSE:U), compared to 23 in the preceding quarter worth $1.54 billion. Jim Davidson, Dave Roux and Glenn Hutchins' Silver Lake Partners held the highest stake in the company, worth approximately $1.13 billion.Similar to Microsoft Corporation (NASDAQ:MSFT), Amazon.com, Inc. (NASDAQ:AMZN), and NVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ:NVDA), Unity Software Inc. (NYSE:U) is a global leader in metaverse advancement.11. These models can then be transformed into immersive virtual reality settings using Autodesk Rendering. Since about 70% of Autodesk, Inc. (NASDAQ:ADSK), compared to 54 funds in the prior quarter. Autodesk, Inc. (NASDAQ:ADSK)’s largest hedge fund investor is Ian Simm’s Impax Asset Management with a $253 million investment.Arch Capital made the following comment about Autodesk, Inc. (NASDAQ:ADSK) in its Q3 2022 investor letter:“Let’s look at a specific example. One of our portfolio companies is Autodesk, Inc. column4: Autodesk CMO on the three things she looks for when building a team
column10: [Autodesk Chief Marketing Officer Dara Treseder has a big job and needs a strong team around her to do it. In an interview with Yahoo Finance from the 2023 Cannes Lions International Festival, Treseder describes the three things she looks for when she builds her teams.Video TranscriptBRIAN SOZZI: I'm Brian Sozzi, here with Brad Smith, at Cannes Lions. And with a very special guest, Autodesk chief marketing officer, Dara Treseder. Dara, good to meet you in person for a change. I'm a LinkedIn fan.DARA TRESEDER: Oh, thank you. Thank you. It's good to meet you in person as well. I'm a Brian fan.BRIAN SOZZI: Oh. No. It's just-- you know what? I appreciate it. Thank you. So Autodesk, I would argue a lot of people here don't even know what Autodesk does. What is it you have to do, as the CMO, to tell people, this is what we do and here's how we change your life?DARA TRESEDER: It's amazing because Autodesk is how the world gets designed and made. Our software is used to make anything. Whether it is cool cars, amazing movies, games, and even the ads that are winning here at Cannes Lion, many of them were made using Autodesk software. And so it's lovely.I think one of the things that's exciting for me as a chief marketing officer, is start to tell the story of the impact Autodesk is having in the world. How we're helping people make better products, how I'm helping people make more sustainable buildings, how we're really helping to drive more impactful outcomes for businesses, products, and the world.BRIAN SOZZI: I followed your career for a while. And I'm not-- not to be bashful or downplay, but Dara is the one that created these Peloton ads. Crushed it as the chief marketing officer over Peloton. How do you take what you learn there and apply it to a software company like this? Are there similarities, are there differences?DARA TRESEDER: There absolutely are similarities. At the end of the day, when I was going over to Peloton, people were like, you're a BW marketer going over to a B2C company. When I was coming over from Peloton to Autodesk, people were like you're a B2C marketer, what are you doing going to market software?Story continuesThe reality is, until ChatGPT takes over, which hasn't happened yet, we are interacting and talking to humans. And so for me, I think the similarity is, at the end of the day, how are you putting your customer at the center of it all? How are you helping drive your customers' outcomes? It's not about what we want to say or what we want to do, it's about what our customers want to get done. And then how we as marketers enable those delightful experiences to make that happen. So that similarities.Of course, there are nuances. Like when you're in a B2C world, it's all about one to many. That's the game. At Autodesk, it's one-to-one and one to many. We definitely have our e-commerce business, which sits on my team. But we also have the one-to-one relationships, right, the account-based marketing. So it's being able to flex between those two things.BRAD SMITH: We've heard a lot of companies talk about how generative AI is going to boost their bottom line at some point in the future. This is something that's already actively in process at Autodesk.DARA TRESEDER: Yes.BRAD SMITH: How have you been able to flip the switch and make sure that people are able to see the difference right now?DARA TRESEDER: I have to give all the credit to our CEO, Andrew. He's just such a visionary. We have a fusion product, which is used to make anything, right. Tesla cars, for example, are designed and made with our software. It has generative AI built into it, and it always has.And so essentially, if you think about it, it's helping you consider alternative possibilities that you may not have thought about yourself. Kind of the way-- you're kind of seeing it more now with ChatGPT, but that generative AI and generative design has been in Autodesk products, and we're continuing to roll out new products to make that happen.For example, we recently launched Forma, our industry cloud for the architecture industry. And instead of starting from scratch, when you're thinking about concept design, AI can help you get there faster. Connecting workflows and removing those repetitive tasks so you can focus on the creative, exciting aspects of your job.BRIAN SOZZI: Where do these ideas come from? Where do you-- like I said, I've followed your career. How do you come up with creative ideas?DARA TRESEDER: You know, I get inspired by impact. I get inspired by connection. I get inspired by stories that cause people to want to leave things better than they found it. Stories that inspire people to do things differently.And I think at the end of the day, when we think about the power of creativity, to me, it's like pixie dust. It's the thing that makes everything fly. It's the magic. And so inspiration can come from anywhere. But at the heart of it, to me, my inspiration comes from driving impact.BRAD SMITH: At the end of the day too, there's so much creativity out there, talent that's here represented at Cannes Lion events. And as you look across your team that you put around you for a lot of these ambitious ventures, what do you look for?DARA TRESEDER: I look for three things. First is courage. Because, I think, when you do the same things, you get the same results. So when you're trying to drive growth, drive a new wave of growth-- right, we've been through so much uncertainty in the world over the past few years. We're still very much in a period of ambiguity and uncertainty in technology. And so having the courage to be able to take some risks, you have to try things, you have to test, you have to experiment. Intuition will drive testing, but then you need to get that data that will inform your decision-making.Conviction is important. You can have courage, but courage without conviction-- you need to have a point of view. Have a North Star, have a place you want to go, and then have the courage to move there.And, of course, confidence. I think confidence is really important. Because it's easy to start something, it's harder to see it through. And so it's being able to bring those three things together to be able to thrive.BRIAN SOZZI: I will just say, before we let you go, I will say, one, I was late to this interview. I'm not Will.I.Am so--BRIAN SOZZI: Some people will actually say, I will be early to my own funeral. So thank you for waiting, one. And it is raining. We're out here in a live environment in the French Riviera, and it's raining. And you know, I know it looks all beautiful. But thank you for rolling with the punches. We appreciate it.DARA TRESEDER: Thank you so much.BRIAN SOZZI: And congratulations on all your success.DARA TRESEDER: Thank you so much. Really glad to be here.]

The top line also improved 13% in constant currency.The company has been benefiting from the robust demand environment as customers are undergoing a major digital transformation. Thus, the rapid adoption of its cloud-based solutions resulted in the better-than-anticipated performance in the fiscal first quarter.Quarterly DetailsComing to CRM’s business segments, revenues from Subscription and Support (93% of the total revenues) increased 11.5% from the year-earlier period to $7.64 billion. Professional Services and Other (7% of total sales) revenues climbed 9% to $605 million.Under the Subscription and Support segment, Sales Cloud revenues grew 10.9% year over year to $1.81 billion. Revenues from Service Cloud, one of the company’s largest and fastest-growing businesses, also improved 11.5% to $1.96 billion.Story continuesMarketing & Commerce Cloud revenues jumped 7.4% to $1.17 billion. Salesforce Platform and Other revenues were up 10.4% to $1.57 billion. Also, revenues from Data increased 18.4% year over year to $1.13 billion.Geographically, Salesforce registered revenue growth of 10.3% in America (66.5% of the total revenues), 16% in the Asia Pacific (9.9%) and 12.3% in the EMEA (23.7%) on a year-over-year basis.Salesforce’s gross profit came in at $6.12 billion, up 14.1% from the prior-year period. Moreover, the non-GAAP operating margin expanded 1,000 bps to 27.6% from 17.6% in the year-ago quarter due to lower operating expenses as a percentage of total sales.
